CHAPTER XVI

Martin Wittenhaagen, standing at the foot of the stairs with his arrow
drawn nearly to the head and his knife behind him, was struck with
amazement to see the men come back without Gerard: he lowered his bow
and looked open-mouthed at them. They, for their part, were equally
puzzled at the attitude they had caught him in.

“Why, mates, was the old fellow making ready to shoot at us?”

“Stuff!” said Martin, recovering his stolid composure; “I was but trying
my new string. There! I'll unstring my bow, if you think that.”

“Humph!” said Dierich suspiciously, “there is something more in you than
I understand: put a log on, and let us dry our hides a bit ere we go.”

A blazing fire was soon made, and the men gathered round it, and their
clothes and long hair were soon smoking from the cheerful blaze. Then it
was that the shrieks were heard in Margaret's room. They all started up,
and one of them seized the candle and ran up the steps that led to the
bedrooms.

Martin rose hastily too, and being confused by these sudden screams, and
apprehending danger from the man's curiosity, tried to prevent him from
going there.

At this Dierich threw his arms round him from behind, and called on the
others to keep him. The man that had the candle got clear away, and all
the rest fell upon Martin, and after a long and fierce struggle, in the
course of which they were more than once all rolling on the floor, with
Martin in the middle, they succeeded in mastering the old Samson, and
binding him hand and foot with a rope they had brought for Gerard.

Martin groaned aloud. He saw the man had made his way to Margaret's room
during the struggle, and here was he powerless.

“Ay, grind your teeth, you old rogue,” said Dierich, panting with the
struggle. “You shan't use them.”

“It is my belief, mates, that our lives were scarce safe while this old
fellow's bones were free.”

“He makes me think this Gerard is not far off,” put in another.

“No such luck,” replied Dierich. “Hallo, mates. Jorian Ketel is a long
time in that girl's bedroom. Best go and see after him, some of us.”

The rude laugh caused by this remark had hardly subsided, when hasty
footsteps were heard running along over head.

“Oh, here he comes, at last. Well, Jorian, what is to do now up there?”

[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

Martin Wittenhaagen stood poised at the base of the staircase, a figure of taut tension, his bowstring pulled tight enough to snap the air, the arrowhead hovering inches from the ceiling, while a dagger rested heavy against his hip. He froze, struck dumb by the absurdity of the scene unfolding above: the men returned, yet Gerard was nowhere to be seen. With a jolt of bewildered realization, he lowered the weapon, his mouth agape, staring upward at the group who now regarded him with equal parts confusion and suspicion.

"Why, mates, was the old fellow making ready to shoot at us?" someone demanded, their voice laced with disbelief.

"Stuff!" Martin retorted, forcing his stolid composure back into place like armor settling over skin. "I was merely testing my new string. There! If you deem it necessary, I will unstring the bow myself."

"Humph!" Dierich grunted, his eyes narrowing with a predatory suspicion that cut deeper than any blade. "There is something more in you than I understand. Put a log on, and let us dry our hides a bit ere we go."

A roaring fire erupted quickly, casting dancing shadows against the rough timber walls. The men clustered around its warmth, the smoke rising from their wet garments and tangled, long hair mingling with the heat. It was amidst this crackling intimacy that the shrieks tore through Margaret's chamber—a sound so primal it shattered the moment. Every head snapped upward. One man snatched the candle, sprinting up the narrow steps toward the sleeping quarters. Martin surged forward, driven by a sudden, visceral dread of the man's intrusive curiosity, attempting to bar his path. But Dierich moved with the speed of a coiled spring, throwing his arms around Martin's waist from behind, shouting orders for the others to hold him fast.

The candle-bearer slipped past the blockade, and the remaining men descended upon Martin. What followed was a chaotic, violent tangle of limbs and fury. For a long, fierce struggle, they rolled across the floorboards, a writhing mass of desperation, with Martin pinned in the center, fighting with the strength of a cornered lion. Yet, they eventually subdued the old Samson, binding his hands and feet tightly with a rope intended for Gerard. Martin groaned aloud, a raw sound of defeat, realizing with horror that the intruder had already breached the sanctuary of Margaret's room while they fought. Now, he was powerless, trapped in the very space he sought to protect.

"Ay, grind your teeth, you old rogue," Dierich panted, his chest heaving from the exertion, his voice dripping with triumph. "You shan't use them."

"It is my belief, mates, that our lives were scarce safe while this old fellow's bones were free," another man observed, wiping sweat from his brow.

"He makes me think this Gerard is not far off," a third added, his tone shifting to one of anxious speculation.

"No such luck," Dierich replied sharply, cutting short the hope. "Hallo, mates. Jorian Ketel has been in that girl's bedroom a long time. Best go and see after him, some of us."

The crude laughter sparked by this remark had barely died away when the sound of hasty footsteps echoed overhead, racing along the gallery.

"Oh, here he comes, at last," Dierich announced, turning toward the stairwell. "Well, Jorian, what is to do now up there?"
